title: How a manufacturer should write an about page
metaTitle: How to write a manufacturer about page
excerpt: Name the people who quote, make, and check the work, and why that matters to a buyer. Keep the origin story only when it changes the decision to inquire.
alt: Hands typing on a laptop at a wooden desk near a window, for a piece on writing an about page a buyer can check.
caption: Someone at the desk, doing the work. An about page should be this specific. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: Who should be named on a manufacturer about page?
faqs.answer: The people who touch an order. Who quotes, who runs the defining process, and who signs inspection. Names are better than departments when they will still be true on the next call. A full staff directory can wait.

faqs.question: When does a founding story belong?
faqs.answer: When deleting it would remove a fact the buyer needs. A specialty that started with a real technical gap, and that still defines the shop, can stay in a few sentences. A garage, a sunrise, and a belief in quality usually do not change the decision to send a drawing.

faqs.question: What should the about page link to?
faqs.answer: The same next step as the rest of the site: talk to sales or download a spec. One proof, where these people made a hard decision, is a useful second link. A unique long form on this page only adds a new obstacle.

sources.title: Influencing your title links in search results

markdown:
A manufacturer about page is proof that specific people stand behind the offer. A buyer who needs specs and confidence wants to know who does the work and why that should matter to their part. They are deciding whether to talk to sales or download a spec. An origin myth that does not change that decision can wait, or it can come off the page.

Write it as an accountability page. Names, roles, place, and the capability those people actually control. The tone can be warm. The facts have to be checkable. A buyer who has been disappointed by a brochure will look here for a human who would answer a hard question about a drawing.

## Who makes the work, who checks it, who replies

Start with the roles that touch an order. Who quotes. Who plans the job. Who runs the process that defines the part. Who signs the inspection. You do not need a full staff directory. You need the buyer to see that the path from their file to a shipped part has people on it, and that those people are allowed to be named.

Names are better than departments when the company is small enough that names are true. A shop of one site can introduce the person who will read the first drawing and the person who owns quality. A larger plant can name the functions and the site, and name a person where a person is the real interface. Inventing a friendly composite spokesperson is a mistake the buyer will catch on the first call.

Say what those people decide. "Mara reviews new drawings before a quote goes out." "The metrology lead signs first-article reports." Role-plus-decision is the sentence that helps. Role-plus-hobby does not. A buyer under time pressure will skip the weekend hiking note and hunt for who owns a nonconformance. Put the ownership where they are already looking.

If the founder still reviews certain jobs, say which ones. If the founder no longer does, do not imply a personal touch the floor cannot deliver. The about page is a promise about attention. Oversell the attention and the first late reply will contradict the site.

## Why this buyer should care

The reason has to connect to their risk. Their risk is a part that arrives wrong, late, or impossible to repeat. The about page should show the experience that reduces that risk. Years on a process, a certification held by a named site, a specialty your generalist competitors avoid, a plant layout that keeps their material traceable. Pick the reasons that are true and relevant to the work you want.

Skip reasons that flatter the company and ignore the buyer. Passion for manufacturing. A belief in quality. A family feeling. Those can be real and still fail to change a purchasing decision. If a family ownership structure matters because the same people will be here for a multi-year tool, say that consequence. The ownership fact earns the sentence. The sentiment does not.

Place matters when place changes the offer. Proximity for a buyer who visits. A port for a buyer who exports. A clean area for a buyer with a contamination spec. A second shift for a buyer with a seasonal spike. State the place and the consequence. A map pin with no implication is scenery.

Equipment belongs here only when it explains the people. "The inspection team runs the CMM the spec assumes" is about accountability. A naked list of machine brands, copied from a capabilities sheet, belongs on the services or spec page. The about page can point there. It should not become a second catalog.

## The origin story, used with a hard test

Keep a founding story when it changes the decision to talk to sales or download a spec. A useful test: if you delete the paragraph, does a serious buyer lose a fact they needed? If the answer is no, cut it or move it to a single line.

Facts that sometimes pass the test are specific. The company started inside a customer's tooling problem and still specializes in that fixture. The metallurgist who founded the shop still writes the weld procedure. The plant was built around a process that is awkward to outsource in pieces. Those facts tell a buyer what kind of judgment they will get.

Facts that fail the test are the common ones. A garage, a borrowed lathe, a first customer who took a chance, a sunrise over the original unit. They may be cherished. They rarely help a stranger choose a supplier. You can keep them for a dinner or a recruiting page. The buyer in a sourcing cycle needs the judgment, the scope, and the next step.

If you tell the story, tell it short, and return to the buyer. Three or four sentences, then what it means for their drawing. A page that spends the first screen on 1987 and mentions the current process in the footer has the order backward.

## Voice, so the page sounds like the shop

Read the homepage, the services list, and the about page in one sitting. They should sound like one company. If the homepage is plain and the about page swells into a manifesto, the buyer hears two authors and trusts neither. Pick the plainer voice. Manufacturing buyers are listening for whether you will be plain when something goes wrong.

Use the words you use in the plant. The process names, the document names, the way you refer to customers. A sudden stack of brand adjectives on this page is a sign the draft was written away from the work. Bring it back. A sentence a supervisor would actually say is the right register.

[Google's guidance on title links](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/title-link) is a small, practical constraint on the top of the page. Give the about page a descriptive title, and one clear main heading. "About us" is a weak heading because it could sit on any company. A heading that names who stands behind the product line is more useful, and it gives search engines a clearer signal than a row of slogans competing for the top of the page.

The same standard of clarity shows up in [Google's people-first content guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content). A reader should be able to tell who is responsible for the work. An about page is the natural place to make that obvious. Name the company, the site, and the people who answer. A page of stock smiles and untitled quotes does not identify anyone.

## Photographs of the work and the people doing it

Use photographs from your floor, with the object in frame when you can. A portrait on a gray seamless backdrop is less persuasive than a person at the bench with the part and the instrument visible. Get permission. Caption the role. A buyer should not have to guess whether the person in the photo still works there.

Reject the factory cliché on this page too. The empty aisle, the handshake in a lobby, the drone roof. They fill space and they dodge the question the page is for. If you cannot photograph the process this quarter, use fewer images and stronger sentences. A thin, true page is better than a thick, generic one.

Thomas Bewick, a public editorial site in Hanabi's work, is a useful comparison from outside manufacturing. It carries a heritage craft by showing the work and the people connected to it, with enough specificity that the history serves the object. Your about page can borrow that standard. History in the service of the part. People in the service of the buyer's decision.

Show the same faces you are willing to put on a call. If the photos are agency models, do not use them. The gap between the site and the kickoff meeting is where confidence dies.

## What the page hands the reader next

End on the action. The buyer who feels the people are real still needs a way to talk to sales or download a spec. Put that step at the end, and once near the top if the page runs long. Repeat the same action the rest of the site uses. A unique "say hello" form that asks for a life story is a new obstacle you added on the one page meant to reduce doubt.

Link to one proof and to the relevant spec. The about page is not the proof page. It can point at a job where these people made a hard decision, and at the file that describes the current offer. A reader who wants more can go deeper. A reader who is ready can act.

Keep contact facts accurate. The plant address if visits happen. The hours a person answers if you publish hours. A phone number only if a person picks it up or returns it. Every fact on this page will be tested by someone. Publish the ones you want tested.

## A short edit before you ship it

Delete any sentence that compliments the company without naming a consequence for the buyer. Delete any claim about speed, size, or care that sales cannot repeat with a straight face. Have the person who answers new inquiries read the page. If they say "we don't really do it that way," believe them and change the page.

Book [an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min) if you want a studio to help you put the accountable version on the site. Bring the current about page, or the list of who actually touches a new drawing. The work is to make those people visible in the same voice as the offer.

A buyer who believes the people are real will ask for evidence from a job. [Proof pages for a manufacturer](/blog/proof-pages-for-a-manufacturer) are the next piece, because a portrait of the team still has to be backed by a constraint, a decision, and the object that left the building.
